title: Chapter 110 — Service, Parts & The Repair Operation
intro: Service models, the repair flow, parts, and the service-sales alliance.

sections.title: Service Models
sections.content:
Some stores have in-house service departments. Others refer to authorized service providers. Know your store's model and how it works.

In-house service gives you control over the customer experience — you can coordinate between the sale, the delivery, and the service call. Third-party service requires clear communication and follow-up because the customer holds you responsible regardless of who does the repair.

sections.title: The Repair Flow
sections.content:
Customer reports a problem. You determine: is it under manufacturer warranty? Under extended warranty? Out of all coverage? Each path is different.

Under manufacturer warranty: contact the manufacturer's service line, provide the model and serial number, schedule the service call. Give the customer the case number.

Under extended warranty: file the claim with the warranty provider, schedule the service, follow up on the timeline.

Out of coverage: connect the customer with a qualified service provider. Provide a realistic cost estimate if you can. This is also the moment to discuss whether repair or replacement makes more economic sense.

sections.title: The Service-Sales Alliance
sections.content:
Service interactions are sales opportunities in disguise. A customer whose 12-year-old fridge needs a $400 compressor repair might be better served by a new $1,200 fridge. Present the option honestly: 'The repair is $400. For that money, you are fixing a 12-year-old fridge that may have other issues coming. A new one with a full warranty starts at $1,200. What makes more sense for you?'

Never pressure. Let the economics speak. The customer who buys a new fridge because the math made sense is satisfied. The one who felt pressured into it is resentful.
